name: Tomas Santos

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for meeting me, Tomas. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no links to AI companies, employers, unions or political parties. Everything you say is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Could you start by describing a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work out of the small depot at the crossroads, covering the coast farms and the fishing villages. Mostly it's repairs. Salt eats the hardware here, so we're always changing insulators and clamps that have gone green. When the winter storms come in off the sea, we're out for days, sleeping in the truck sometimes.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what's hard?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that it's honest work. You fix something, the lights come back, and people thank you at Mass on Sunday. What's hard is the pay, which is lower out here than in the towns, and there's nothing else like it nearby. I rent a small cottage two doors from my parents, and I've got maybe two or three weeks of money saved. I help my uncle on his farm on weekends, which helps a bit.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Do you use any AI tools?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: No. I don't have any of that on my phone, and I don't want it. My little nephew showed me one once and it told him a lie with a straight face. That was enough for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, I never trusted it. At the depot we'd say the same thing. I don't go online much, but my mother would tell the neighbours I was right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, same thing. It's a relief. My job is climbing poles near the sea, and no computer was going to do that anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going like now. Work, help my uncle on the farm on Saturdays, go to church on Sunday. Try to put a bit aside each month, maybe fifty, because the cottage roof needs work and the landlord is slow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like a quiet Sunday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said your nephew's AI told a lie. What happened?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He asked it about our village, and it said there was a castle here. There's no castle, there's a church and a fish market. If it can't get my village right, I'm not letting it near a live line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is the money worry bigger than any AI worry?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, much bigger. The landlord, the car insurance, my mother's medicines when my father's pension runs short. That's what I think about, not computers.

S0.say: Good, he never trusted it, and his crew would agree. He's rarely online, but his mother would tell the neighbours he was right.
S0.think: It's a relief, because climbing poles by the sea was never something a computer would do. His real worries are about money.
S0.do: Keeps working, helps his uncle on the farm on Saturdays and goes to church on Sundays. Tries to save about fifty a month for repairs on his rented cottage.
S0.quote: If it can't get my village right, I'm not letting it near a live line.
S0.fieldNote: Tomas's distrust of AI comes from one concrete moment: a chatbot inventing a castle in his village. His world is tightly tied to family, church and the coast. Money for his parents' medicines weighs on him more than technology.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say let the office people worry about it. Out here, someone still has to climb the pole in the rain. I'd say that at the depot and to the men after Mass.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm not so sure. I've seen the drones they fly along the big lines now. If they start sending drones to find faults instead of us driving the coast road, maybe they need fewer of us. And I'm not good with screens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and watch what happens. I wouldn't go to any computer course unless they made me. I'd do a bit more on my uncle's farm, so I have something if the hours get cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. A bit of worry, but I'd put it in God's hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the hours got cut, what would you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ask my uncle for more days on the farm. Ask the priest if anyone in the parish needs a strong pair of hands. Out here you don't go to the government office, you go to your family and your parish.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame if crews got cut?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The big tech companies, selling something people don't need. And the managers in the city who believe them. The company used to be run by people who'd climbed a pole.

S1.say: Let the office people worry; out here someone still has to climb the pole in the rain. He'd say that at the depot and after Mass.
S1.think: He's less sure in private, having seen drones on the big lines. If drones find faults instead of crews driving the coast road, fewer workers might be needed, and he's not good with screens.
S1.do: Keeps working and waits to see what happens, avoiding computer courses unless required. Takes more days on his uncle's farm as a backup.
S1.feel: Uneasy, but he'd put it in God's hands.
S1.quote: Out here you don't go to the government office, you go to your family and your parish.
S1.fieldNote: The gap between his public confidence and private doubt is clear here. His safety net is family and parish, not the state, and he says so proudly. He blames tech companies and city managers, not the people on the ground.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. This is AGI by 2028. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's wrong, and people should stop buying from companies that throw workers away. I'd say it at the depot and at church, and I'd tell the priest it should be talked about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be frightened. Two weeks of money, no other line company, and if robots can climb a pole they can probably pick olives too. My uncle's farm wouldn't save me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd give up the cottage and move back with my parents, which would save most of my rent. I'd cut everything else. I'd work every hour I could get while the job lasts, and lean on the family and the parish. I wouldn't take a handout unless there was truly nothing else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened. Like a storm that doesn't stop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you wouldn't take a handout. If it came to it, would you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If my mother needed her medicines and there was no other way, yes. I'd be ashamed, but yes. I'd take the help for my mother before I'd take it for myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your father?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him I'm moving back for a while, to help with the house. He'd know the real reason. He'd say we'll manage, like we always have, and he'd mean it.

S2.say: It's wrong, and people should stop buying from companies that throw workers away. He'd say so at the depot and at church, and ask the priest to raise it.
S2.think: He'd be frightened, with two weeks of money and no other line employer, and robots that could also do farm work, so his uncle's farm wouldn't save him.
S2.do: Gives up the cottage to move back with his parents and cuts all other spending. Works every hour available while the job lasts and leans on family and parish, taking state help only as a last resort.
S2.feel: Frightened, like a storm that doesn't stop.
S2.quote: I'd take the help for my mother before I'd take it for myself.
S2.fieldNote: His pride against handouts bends only for his mother. He'd move back home quickly and frame it as helping his parents. The farm fallback he relied on in the gentler scenario disappears here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now AGI by 2031. The same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is time for families to get ready. Save, help each other, look after the old ones. That's what I'd say at church.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years doesn't fix much for me. I'm not going to become a computer man. But I could save something and maybe help my uncle buy a machine or two for the farm, so the family has something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save every month, maybe a hundred if I gave up eating out and the car I don't really need. I'd keep working the lines. I'd talk to my uncle about going in together on the farm, so it supports more of us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but steadier than with the fast one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would this change any personal plans, like marriage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's a girl from the parish, Inês. We've been courting a year. With five years, I think I'd ask her sooner, not later. A family is the one thing a robot can't take from you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd help your uncle buy machines. Isn't that the same thing you're worried about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. But it's our machine, on our land. That's different from a company in the city replacing us. If it keeps the family fed, I'd do it.

S3.say: Five years is time for families to get ready by saving, helping each other and looking after the elderly. That's what he'd say at church.
S3.think: Five years doesn't change much for him since he won't become 'a computer man', but he could save and help his uncle make the farm support more of the family.
S3.do: Saves about a hundred a month by cutting meals out and selling a car he doesn't need. Keeps working the lines, plans to go in with his uncle on the farm, and would propose to Inês sooner.
S3.feel: Anxious, but steadier than in the fast scenario.
S3.quote: A family is the one thing a robot can't take from you.
S3.fieldNote: Family is his answer to almost everything, including whether to marry sooner. He separates a family-owned machine from a company replacing workers, which is a telling line. He won't retrain into technology.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one, AGI by 2036. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough for families and communities to prepare without asking the government for everything. Teach the young ones a trade, keep the land.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be thirty-seven, hopefully married with a child or two. Ten years is long enough that I'd probably keep working most of it. But I'd always know it's coming, and that would sit on me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and keep saving, a little every month. I'd marry and try to build a family in the village. I'd keep helping my uncle and learn more about the farm, so there's something to fall back on if the line work goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Something in the back of the mind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you want your own children to go into line work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it still existed, yes, it's good work. But I'd want them to know the farm too. My grandfather said always have two things you can do with your hands. I think he was right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd teach them the farm, even though robots might do that too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe they will. I don't know. But land is land. Even if a machine works it, someone owns it. I'd want that to be us.

S4.say: Ten years is enough for families and communities to prepare without asking the government for everything. Teach the young a trade and keep the land.
S4.think: He'd be 37 and hopefully married with children, and would probably keep working most of the decade, though knowing it's coming would weigh on him.
S4.do: Keeps working and saving a little each month, marries and builds a family in the village. Keeps helping his uncle and learns more about farming as a fallback.
S4.feel: Uneasy, with something at the back of his mind.
S4.quote: My grandfather said always have two things you can do with your hands. I think he was right.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years he thinks in generations: land, family and his grandfather's advice. He doesn't claim to know whether robots will farm too, but values owning the land. He still won't turn to technology himself.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. No time to save, no time to plan, and my parents depending on me. What would help is the company keeping on the men it has, and if not, paying for apprenticeships in something real, a trade with tools. Not just sending money and telling people to sit at home.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about the storms. When the sea comes over the wall in January, nobody in the village cares how clever the machine is. They want to know someone's coming. That should count for something.

headlineQuote: When the sea comes over the wall in January, nobody in the village cares how clever the machine is. They want to know someone's coming.
portrait: Tomas is a 27-year-old lineworker on a small depot covering coast farms and fishing villages, where salt eats the hardware and winter storms keep crews out for days. He rents a cottage two doors from his parents, helps his uncle's farm on weekends and has two or three weeks of money saved. He doesn't use AI, distrusts it, and turns to family, parish and the land before the government. He's calm through AI Plateau and uneasy about Steady Disruption, while AGI by 2028 frightens him because even the farm wouldn't save him. With more time, he thinks in terms of family: saving, marrying sooner and keeping land in the family.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because there would be no time to save or plan and his parents depend on him.
whatWouldHelp: The company keeping on the workers it has, or paying for apprenticeships in a real trade with tools, rather than sending money and telling people to stay home.
